title: How to Tell if Eggs Are Bad

seo.title: How to Tell if Eggs Are Bad
seo.meta_description: How to tell if eggs are bad, which signs matter, and why the float test cannot prove an egg is safe.
seo.search_intent: Resolve the household question clearly and safely, with practical decision points and next steps.

excerpt: The float test mainly suggests age, not safety. Storage history, shell condition, date, smell, and appearance are more useful clues.
content_html:
No home test can turn an egg with an unknown storage history into a guaranteed safe egg. The useful decision combines storage history, shell condition, date, and what you observe after cracking it. The familiar float test can suggest age, but it does not prove an egg is free of harmful bacteria.

Start with how the eggs were stored

If they were sold refrigerated, keep them refrigerated. An egg that spent too long at an unsafe temperature does not become safe because it sinks in water.

Discard cracked shells

The FDA recommends buying clean, uncracked eggs. A crack gives microorganisms an easier path from the outside of the shell to the contents.

Crack a questionable egg into a separate bowl

If quality is uncertain, open it into a small cup or bowl before adding it to other ingredients. A distinctly rotten or unpleasant odor after cracking is enough reason to discard it.

Some visual changes are normal

USDA guidance notes that a cloudy white can be a sign of freshness and that a small blood spot does not by itself make an egg unsafe. A pink or iridescent egg white, however, can indicate bacterial spoilage and should be discarded.

The float test is mostly an age test

As an egg ages, its air cell grows and the egg may become more buoyant. That can help estimate age, but it is not a microbiological safety test. An egg that sinks can still have been stored improperly.

When the history is unknown, do not guess

If you do not know how long the eggs have been stored, the refrigerator lost power, or they sat out for many hours, discarding them is safer than trying to pass them with a kitchen trick.

Egg safety is largely determined before you crack the shell: purchase, temperature, and storage. Smell and appearance can reveal spoilage, but they do not replace safe handling.

faq.question: Does a floating egg mean it is bad?
faq.answer: Floating mainly reflects a larger air cell as the egg ages. It is not a sufficient safety test.

faq.question: Does a blood spot mean the egg is spoiled?
faq.answer: Not by itself. USDA guidance says a small blood spot does not make an egg unsafe.

faq.question: Is a pink egg white normal?
faq.answer: No. USDA guidance associates pink or iridescent whites with bacterial spoilage, so discard the egg.
